sections.model_projection: The model projects Denver 22.03, Kansas City 21.12, a margin of roughly 1 point in favor of the visiting Broncos. The projected total is 43.15 against a market total of 43.5. Kansas City's win probability sits at 43.5%, meaning the model gives Denver a slight edge despite the Chiefs being 3-point home favorites. The model's margin differs from the market spread by 3.9 points in Denver's direction.
sections.offensive_matchup: Both offenses are statistically modest, with Kansas City averaging 21.3 points per game (rank 20) and Denver at 23.2 (rank 15). Denver's defense is the sharper unit here: its defensive EPA per play (a measure of how many expected points an opponent gains per snap) sits at -0.062, ranking 7th, while Kansas City's defensive EPA per play is +0.009, ranking 16th, meaning the Chiefs' defense has actually been a slight net negative. Denver's defensive success rate — the share of opponent plays that generate positive EPA — is 37.8% allowed (rank 2), compared to Kansas City's 44.9% allowed (rank 20), a meaningful gap that suggests Denver will be better at keeping Chiefs drives from gaining traction on a play-by-play basis. Kansas City's offense runs at a fast pace (rank 3 in seconds per play) and passes at the second-highest neutral-script rate in the league at 65.6%, setting up a direct confrontation with Denver's pass defense.
sections.quarterback_edge: Patrick Mahomes holds a clear career edge over Bo Nix: Mahomes has a career EPA per dropback of 0.154 across 93 games and 3,447 attempts, compared to Nix's 0.055 across 36 games and 1,251 attempts. Mahomes also averages 7.34 yards per attempt versus Nix's 6.5. The quarterback edge is the single largest factor favoring Kansas City in the model, contributing 0.52 points toward the Chiefs. However, Mahomes will face the NFL's top-ranked pass-rush unit by pressure rate (32.2%) and the top-ranked sack rate defense (9.87% sack rate), which partially offsets his individual advantage.
sections.trenches: The offensive line matchup is one of the most decisive edges in this game, favoring Denver by a score of -2 (away-favored). Kansas City's offensive line allowed sacks on 6.82% of dropbacks (rank 20), while Denver's defensive front generates pressure on 32.2% of dropbacks — the best rate in the league — and does so without blitzing at the top rate in the league (20.9% pressure without blitz, rank 1). Denver's pass protection is also strong, allowing sacks on just 3.41% of dropbacks (rank 2), while Kansas City's pass rush generates sacks on only 6.0% of opponent dropbacks (rank 19). In the run game, Kansas City's offensive line yards (3.01, rank 8) are better than Denver's (2.76, rank 21), but Denver's run defense holds opponents to 2.66 line yards allowed (rank 6), limiting that advantage.
sections.explosive_play_edge: Denver holds an edge in the explosive play category, both generating and suppressing big plays better than Kansas City. Denver's defense allows explosive plays (10-plus rushing or 20-plus passing yards) on just 6.34% of opponent snaps, the best rate in the league, while Kansas City's offense generates explosives on only 7.34% of plays (rank 26). Denver's own offense produces explosives at an 8.11% rate (rank 20), which is modest, but Kansas City's defense allows them on 7.93% of plays (rank 11). The net effect is that this game is unlikely to be decided by chunk plays, but Denver is better positioned to prevent the big-play moments that can swing outcomes.
sections.third_down_red_zone: Denver owns a significant structural advantage on third downs and in the red zone. Denver's defense holds opponents to a 35.7% third-down conversion rate (rank 5), while Kansas City's defense allows conversions at a 44.1% rate (rank 28, among the worst in the league). Offensively, Denver converts at 42.0% (rank 8) versus Kansas City's 38.4% (rank 21). In the red zone, Denver scores touchdowns on 62.7% of trips (rank 15) and holds opponents to touchdowns on just 49.4% of their red-zone visits (rank 4), while Kansas City scores touchdowns on only 55.9% of trips (rank 22) and allows them on 57.4% (rank 12). These gaps compound: Denver is more likely to convert drives into points and more likely to force Kansas City into field goal attempts.
sections.roster_talent: Denver enters with a roster continuity index of 0.98 and returning production of 97% overall, including 100% of passing production and 98% of receiving production returning. Kansas City's continuity index is 0.86, with total returning production at 71%, including only 30% of rushing production and 57% of defensive production returning. This gives Denver a meaningful familiarity edge, contributing -0.24 points toward Kansas City in the model. Talent ratings are unavailable for both teams per the data package.

sections.expected_game_script: This game figures to be a low-scoring, defense-influenced contest given both offenses rank outside the top 14 in EPA per play and the projected total sits at 43.15. Kansas City will lean heavily on passing — their neutral-script pass rate of 65.6% is second in the league — but they will run directly into Denver's elite pass-rush front, which generates pressure on nearly a third of dropbacks without needing to blitz. Mahomes' experience and improvisation ability will be tested by that pressure, and his offensive line's vulnerability to sacks (rank 20) is a genuine concern. Denver's offense, led by Nix, will face a Kansas City blitz package (rank 2 at 41.1% blitz rate) that could create uncomfortable situations for a quarterback with 36 career games of experience. The third-down and red-zone edges both favor Denver structurally, meaning that even if Kansas City moves the ball, they may settle for field goals more often than touchdowns. The game is likely to stay close into the fourth quarter, with Denver's defensive consistency giving them a slight edge to cover the margin, though Mahomes' individual quality keeps Kansas City in position to win outright at home.
